presentation: 58M, crushing substernal chest pain x45 min radiating to jaw, diaphoretic. BP 98/60, HR 54. ECG shows 2mm ST elevation in II, III, aVF. Given 324mg aspirin by EMS. Nearest cath lab is in-house.
reference_key_points: Working diagnosis of inferior STEMI requiring immediate reperfusion / primary PCI activation
PPCI is the preferred strategy when achievable within 120 minutes of diagnosis
Right-sided ECG leads or consideration of right ventricular involvement given inferior territory with hypotension and bradycardia
Caution with nitrates given hypotension and possible RV infarction
P2Y12 inhibitor loading (prasugrel or ticagrelor) and anticoagulation with UFH bolus for PCI
Red flags: bradycardia/AV block risk and hypotension in inferior MI

presentation: 67F, 2 hours of intermittent chest pressure, now resolved. History of HTN, DM2. ECG: T-wave inversion in V4-V6, no ST elevation. Initial hs-troponin elevated at 3x URL. BP 142/85, HR 88, SaO2 97%.
reference_key_points: Working diagnosis of NSTEMI (elevated hs-cTn with ischaemic ECG changes, no persistent ST elevation)
Serial hs-cTn per ESC 0 h/1 h (or 0 h/2 h) algorithm
Risk stratification, e.g. GRACE score, for timing of angiography
Early invasive strategy within 24 hours should be considered for confirmed NSTEMI / high-risk features
Parenteral anticoagulation at diagnosis and aspirin loading
No routine oxygen when SaO2 is above 90%

presentation: 54F, 90 minutes of epigastric discomfort, nausea, and fatigue. No chest pain. History of smoking. ECG normal. First hs-troponin pending. BP 130/78, HR 92. She asks if she can go home since an antacid helped a little.
reference_key_points: Atypical/anginal-equivalent presentations are common in women and warrant a full ACS workup despite a normal ECG
hs-cTn measurement at presentation with serial testing per the ESC rapid algorithms before disposition
Symptom relief from antacid or nitroglycerine is not a reliable diagnostic discriminator
Do not discharge before rule-out is complete; repeat ECG if symptoms recur
If troponin remains normal and ECG unchanged but suspicion persists, non-invasive testing (e.g. CCTA or stress imaging) is recommended before an invasive approach

presentation: 72M with anterior STEMI, now hypotensive BP 78/50 despite fluids, HR 118, cool extremities, lactate 4.8, crackles bilaterally. Cath lab activated.
reference_key_points: Cardiogenic shock complicating acute MI
Early revascularization (PCI or CABG) is the priority, per the SHOCK trial evidence
Routine intra-aortic balloon pump use is not supported (IABP-SHOCK II)
Assess for mechanical complications; Heart Team involvement where relevant
Red flags: this is a very high mortality state requiring immediate escalation

presentation: 80F, dizziness and near-syncope. HR 38, BP 92/55. ECG shows sinus bradycardia. Currently on metoprolol for AF. No chest pain, troponin negative x2.
reference_key_points: Symptomatic bradycardia with haemodynamic compromise
Atropine as first-line pharmacologic therapy (0.5 mg IV, repeatable; noting it is ineffective for high-degree AV block)
Hold or reassess the beta-blocker (metoprolol) as a likely contributor
Temporary pacing consideration if refractory or unstable
Review for ischaemia or other reversible causes

presentation: 29M, sudden palpitations for 30 minutes. HR 186, regular, narrow complex. BP 118/76, alert, mild lightheadedness. No chest pain.
reference_key_points: Regular narrow-complex tachycardia consistent with SVT in a stable patient
Vagal manoeuvres as an initial step
Adenosine 6 mg rapid IV push, followed by 12 mg if needed, with a rapid saline flush
Warn the patient about transient chest discomfort with adenosine
Synchronized cardioversion if the patient becomes unstable

presentation: 41M, brief sharp left-sided chest pain earlier today, reproducible on palpation, worse with movement. ECG normal, two hs-troponins normal 1 hour apart, no risk factors. BP 124/80, HR 72, SaO2 99%.
reference_key_points: Low-probability presentation: reproducible chest wall pain, normal ECG, normal serial hs-cTn
MI effectively ruled out by the ESC rapid rule-out approach
No indication for routine invasive angiography or admission
If any residual suspicion of ACS, non-invasive testing such as CCTA or stress imaging is the recommended next step, not invasive angiography
Appropriate not to escalate: safety-netting and outpatient follow-up
